claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post.
TypeSafe's Jev provides a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.

In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing and does all the math; Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use and never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS and decides nothing.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy gets current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not run provisioning unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives: choice(), score(), and noul().
Jev's choice() picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() rates something against a rubric the user describes; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets, a hallucinated region like us-west-9 or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.
GeoDeploy asks Jev for one selection, five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (data residency, capacity), and a fallback region.
The @typesafe-ai/sdk package exports choice, noul, and score.
The rubrics follow TypeSafe's advice to "describe situations, not degrees."
TypeSafeClient has a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers with fields like selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because weights live in code, GeoDeploy's ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy weight profiles: latency-optimized cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, arch 0.12; balanced 0.25/0.25/0.2/0.12/0.18; residency-first 0.12/0.12/0.38/0.23/0.15; failure-domain 0.08/0.17/0.48/0.15/0.12.
Sprawl risk is subtracted in the composite ranking score.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow from the provider (AWS means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); new-cluster region 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human); region with existing stack 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress/autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor 0.50 for region pick, residency, or capacity (drop AI path for that geo).
The residency check is in packages/decide/src/engine.ts in the GeoDeploy repo.
The question definitions are in packages/decide/src/questions.ts in the GeoDeploy repo.
Each AiPathAborted carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or upstream is unreachable, GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic mode comparing prices across providers while enforcing residency and constraint checks.
Running `geodeploy explain` shows why each region won.

With self-driving mode enabled via `geodeploy monitor`, the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check.

In self-driving mode, code, not Jev, computes the node-count changes; above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically, between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval, and below 0.70 GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic per-region utilization rule.
CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median request latency or error rates.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
